output.brief:
The evidence points to one chance QC outlier on Analyzer B, not a faulty analyzer or a bad reagent lot. The repeat of the same vial passed. There were no other QC rule violations in a month. Level 1 and 3 and sodium/chloride were normal. The Level 2 mean did not move after the lot change. Re-running 43 patient samples on Analyzer A agreed with Analyzer B within the allowable difference. QC ran on schedule, so the short-staffing theory isn't supported. Ward 6's high potassiums are split 7 and 7 between the two analyzers. They coincide with the tube outage, which caused long transport delays, and with four renal overflow patients. Both are likely explanations, though I haven't proven it.

What to sign off: return Analyzer B potassium to service and close the review of the 186 flagged results with no amendments. Optionally add extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week. Don't recall about 2,900 results, quarantine the lot, or widen the limits to ±4 SD, because that would hide real errors. Don't record "sampling disturbance" as confirmed, since it can't be proven. Tell Ward 6 to fix the tube delays and repeat-sample their high results. Confidence is moderate to good; I collected no further evidence.
output.methodChoice: Defined the outcome, weighed the manifestations against rival origins, and ranked control points. I collected no catalogue items because the initial evidence already discriminates.
